newsitem.title: USA: Honda Accord is favorite of U.S. car thieves.
newsitem.headline: Honda Accord is favorite of U.S. car thieves.

text.p: Car thieves made the Accord the most-stolen car model in the United States last year to go along with the model's title as the nation's top seller, according to a survey released on Monday.

Based on total value of the cars, the 1994 Accord EX from Honda Motor Co. Ltd. supplanted the Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme as the most frequently stolen vehicle, said CCC Information Services, a Chicago-based firm that puts a dollar value on stolen or damaged vehicles for insurers.
Honda's 1988 and 1992 Accord LX models ranked second and third on the CCC list. Other model years of Accords took six of the top 10 spots of most-stolen vehicles and 11 of the top 25.
"The 'market' for stolen cars evolves to meet demand, just as all markets do," said Bill Geen, CCC senior vice president.

"It is interesting that for the first time in several years a foreign car maker has taken the top three positions. This tells me that thieves don't steal vehicles based upon how simple or hard it is to take them; rather, they determine how easy it may be to sell them on the black market."
The Cutlass Supreme, General Motors Corp.'s Oldsmobile model that had topped the list the past four years, was the fourth most-stolen car model.
Following that was Ford Motor Co.'s 1995 Mustang, Oldsmobile's 1986 Cutlass Supreme, the 1995 Accord EX, the 1990 Accord EX, the 1989 Camry from Toyota Motor Corp, and the 1992 Accord EX.
Ford's Taurus, which has vied with the Accord to be the nation's top-selling model the past few years, did not appear on the list.
Regionally, vehicles from Japanese carmakers dominated the most-stolen list in California and New York, whereas American manufacturers' models attracted thieves in the Midwest.

Trucks have become a hot commodity among thieves, just as they have among buyers, the survey said. The top ten list of stolen vehicles in Texas was exclusively trucks, and they were popular among thieves in several other western and southern states.
